lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: In 1930, a famous economist predicted we'd only need to work fifteen hours a week. Most of us have done that by Tuesday afternoon.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: The forty-hour week isn't a law of nature. Henry Ford adopted it in 1926, arguing that people with free time buy more cars.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Parkinson's law says work expands to fill the time available. His example: the Admiralty gained officials while losing two thirds of its ships.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Add an average American commute of twenty-seven minutes each way. And Gallup finds only twenty percent of employees worldwide are engaged at work.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: When sixty-one British companies tried a four-day week in 2022, fifty-six kept it going, revenue held steady, and sick days fell by sixty-five percent.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: But steady jobs have a real case. About half of new American businesses are gone within five years, and in Britain the self-employed get no statutory sick pay.

lines.speaker: benny
lines.text: So the trap comes with dental.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: And when an Austrian village lost its factory in 1929, researchers found the unemployed men walked slower, and most weren't even wearing a watch.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: The forty-hour week was a victory. The trap is treating a deal from the nineteen-twenties like a law of nature.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Is yours a trap or a good deal? The full story is on our channel.
